connection: Session 33 registered the complete persistence graph directly in Web Program.cs. Those registrations work. Session 34A groups their detailed recipe behind one Infrastructure extension method and proves the graph can be constructed.
objectives: Identify Web Program.cs as the composition root.
Extract EF Core, repository, and AsyncClockEntryService registrations into Infrastructure/ServiceRegistration.cs.
Explain why the DbContext graph uses scoped lifetimes.
Verify transitive constructor resolution through a real service provider.

visuals.title: Composition root and recipe
visuals.explanation: Program.cs chooses the application configuration; AddTimeClockPersistence organizes the detailed persistence recipe without becoming the composition root.

visuals.title: Constructor-resolution chain
visuals.explanation: Resolving AsyncClockEntryService requires IAsyncClockEntryRepository, then EfClockEntryRepository, then TimeClockDbContext.

visuals.title: One request, one scope
visuals.explanation: Services registered with AddScoped are reused inside one request scope and replaced in a later request scope.

visuals.title: Construction evidence
visuals.explanation: A passing resolution test proves the graph can be constructed, while behavioral and database claims remain outside its evidence.

preQuiz.prompt: Why is Program.cs still the composition root after registration details move to an extension method?
options: Program.cs still chooses which recipe and connection string the application uses
Every extension method is automatically a composition root
preQuiz.explanation: The final application-level choices remain in Program.cs.

preQuiz.prompt: What happens if EfClockEntryRepository is not registered?
preQuiz.explanation: The container cannot complete the transitive constructor chain.

preQuiz.prompt: What does AddScoped promise inside one scope?
options: Repeated resolutions reuse one scoped instance
Every resolution creates an unrelated provider
preQuiz.explanation: Scoped services are reused within a scope and replaced across scopes.

concept.title: Working code can still be organized
paragraphs: Session 33's registrations in Program.cs work and are not inherently wrong. Program.cs is the composition root because it makes final application choices: which implementation graph to use and which SQLite connection string to supply.

ServiceRegistration.cs groups the persistence recipe behind AddTimeClockPersistence. The extension method organizes composition details; it does not become the composition root because it does not choose whether the Web application uses that recipe or what configuration value to pass.

concept.title: Resolution follows constructors transitively
paragraphs: GetRequiredService<AsyncClockEntryService> asks the provider to construct the service. Its constructor requires IAsyncClockEntryRepository, whose registered implementation is EfClockEntryRepository, whose constructor requires TimeClockDbContext.

The chain is AsyncClockEntryService → IAsyncClockEntryRepository → EfClockEntryRepository → TimeClockDbContext. If any required registration is absent, GetRequiredService throws instead of returning a partly constructed graph.

concept.title: Scoped lifetime matches request work
paragraphs: AddScoped reuses one instance of each scoped service inside one scope. A different scope receives different instances.

ASP.NET Core normally creates one scope per HTTP request. A scoped DbContext therefore tracks one request's unit of work and is disposed with that request. Repository and service instances resolved in the same request share the appropriate scoped dependencies.

concept.title: A composition test checks construction, not behavior
paragraphs: The test creates a real ServiceCollection, applies the registration extension, builds a provider, creates a scope, and resolves AsyncClockEntryService.

Passing proves the dependency graph can be constructed. It does not prove clock-in behavior, SQL correctness, persistence, or HTTP behavior; those require behavioral or integration tests with different evidence.

lab.title: Extract and verify the persistence registration recipe
lab.objective: Centralize the existing persistence registrations without moving application-level choices out of Program.cs.
lab.task: Create AddTimeClockPersistence, use it from Web, and prove AsyncClockEntryService resolves through the complete constructor chain.
lab.startingCondition: Web Program.cs contains working AddDbContext and AddScoped calls from Session 33.

steps.text: In Infrastructure, create ServiceRegistration.cs and type a public static ServiceRegistration class. A static class is appropriate because this file holds stateless extension methods and is never instantiated.
steps.completeWhen: The new file contains the empty public static class.

steps.text: Add the required Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore and Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection using directives. Then use a comment-first scaffold for public static IServiceCollection AddTimeClockPersistence(this IServiceCollection services, string connectionString). Temporarily return services.
steps.completeWhen: The warning-free extension-method shell returns the same collection.

steps.text: Inside AddTimeClockPersistence, register TimeClockDbContext with AddDbContext and configure UseSqlite(connectionString). Keep the provider configuration attached to the registration.
steps.completeWhen: The method contains a configured SQLite DbContext registration.

steps.text: Register IAsyncClockEntryRepository to EfClockEntryRepository with AddScoped. The interface request now maps to the concrete implementation for one scope.
steps.completeWhen: The repository mapping appears exactly once.

steps.text: Register AsyncClockEntryService with AddScoped, then return services. Returning the same collection permits normal registration chaining.
steps.completeWhen: The complete extension method registers the DbContext, repository, and service and returns services.
steps.purposeAfter: Infrastructure now owns the detailed persistence recipe, while callers remain free to choose whether and how to apply it.

steps.text: In Web Program.cs, replace only the three detailed persistence registrations with builder.Services.AddTimeClockPersistence("Data Source=timeclock.db"). Keep AddControllers, Build, startup initialization, MapControllers, and Run in their existing order.
steps.completeWhen: Program.cs makes one persistence-registration call and still chooses the connection string.

steps.text: Explain the boundary before building: Program.cs remains the composition root because it selects AddTimeClockPersistence and supplies application configuration. ServiceRegistration only packages the selected recipe.
steps.completeWhen: You can explain why moving details did not move the composition root.
steps.purposeAfter: The refactor changes organization, not dependency direction or runtime behavior.

steps.text: Build the Web project in Release to verify the extension method is visible and Program.cs still composes successfully.
steps.completeWhen: The Web build succeeds with zero errors.

steps.text: In the test project, create ServiceRegistrationTests.cs and an xUnit Fact named AddTimeClockPersistence_WhenGraphIsComplete_ResolvesAsyncClockEntryService. Create a real ServiceCollection and call AddTimeClockPersistence with Data Source=:memory:.
steps.completeWhen: The test has a configured ServiceCollection before provider construction.

steps.text: Build an explicitly typed ServiceProvider, create an explicitly typed IServiceScope, and resolve AsyncClockEntryService from scope.ServiceProvider with GetRequiredService.
steps.completeWhen: Resolution crosses the real transitive constructor chain inside a scope.

steps.text: Assert that the resolved service is not null. State the evidence accurately: this proves graph construction, not clock-in or database behavior.
steps.completeWhen: The assertion and its limited meaning are both present.
steps.purposeAfter: A missing DbContext, repository mapping, or service registration now causes focused composition-test failure.

steps.text: Run the focused composition test, build the complete Release solution, then run the complete suite with --no-build.
steps.code:
dotnet test tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj --configuration Release --filter FullyQualifiedName~ServiceRegistrationTests
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release
dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build
steps.completeWhen: The focused test and complete suite pass after the matching Release build.

lab.expectedBehavior: The Web host uses one registration extension, and the composition test proves the complete scoped constructor graph can be resolved.
lab.validation:
dotnet test tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj --configuration Release --filter FullyQualifiedName~ServiceRegistrationTests
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release
dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

expectedFiles.why: Choose and invoke the registration recipe from the composition root.
Verify transitive constructor resolution inside a scope.

commit: session-34a: centralize and verify persistence registration
review: Program.cs still makes final application choices.
The extension method groups details without becoming the composition root.
DbContext, repository, and service are scoped.
The test resolves through a real provider scope.
The test claims only construction evidence, not behavior.

postQuiz.explanation: It groups composition details behind one descriptive call.

postQuiz.prompt: What does the composition test prove?
options: The registered constructor graph can be constructed
postQuiz.explanation: Resolution evidence is narrower than behavioral evidence.

postQuiz.prompt: Why create a scope in the test?
options: To resolve scoped services within their intended lifetime boundary
postQuiz.explanation: Scoped services belong to a scope, just as they do during an HTTP request.

reflections: Which decision keeps Program.cs the composition root?
Which missing registration would break each link in the resolution chain?
What additional test would be required to prove actual persistence behavior?
whatBreaks: Omitting any registration breaks GetRequiredService. Registering the DbContext with an inappropriate lifetime can leak tracking state across requests. Moving the connection-string choice into Infrastructure would blur the composition-root boundary.
summary: Session 34A centralizes the working persistence recipe and proves its complete scoped constructor graph resolves.
